catalog_quote: 2.2 Phonotactics • No monomoraic words are attested, but bimoraic monosyllabic words are, e.g., ɗiː ‘pepper’ • Attested syllable shapes are V, CV, CVN, CVV, and CVVN ... 2.4 Stress • There is a stress system consisting of trochaic feet – [ˈmitʃu] ‘mosquito’ – [iˈɓʲatʃu] ‘shrimp’ – [makaˈʃiʝ(V)] ‘sweet manioc’ • Alignment of feet with a word edge is not discernible from present data • Syllables containing nasal codas, diphthongs, and/or long vowels attract stress [fn. 1: A ‘V’ in parentheses in this document indexes the presence of an indiscernible final vowel.]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Atorai has word stress organized in trochaic feet; heavy syllables (CVN, CVV with diphthong or long vowel) attract stress; the author explicitly cannot determine from the 1965 archival recordings which word edge the feet align to, so no fixed default position is stated (examples show initial, second-syllable and final stress).
new_statements.exceptions: None beyond the statement that edge alignment is not discernible; data are ~2.5 h of 1965 lexical elicitation (G. Kingsley Noble reel tapes, Survey of California and Other Indian Languages), with frequent word-final vowel (and sometimes final-syllable) devoicing.
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated words/short phrases from lexical elicitation (citation forms); word-level stress marks in phonetic transcriptions.
new_statements.identity_note: Both modern sources describe 'Atorai' as recorded by G. Kingsley Noble in 1965 in the Rupununi basin, Guyana (Glottolog ator1244 Atorada, ISO aox). Ramirez 2001 treats Atorai as a possible dialect of Wapixana (wapi1253) but O'Hagan and Miller treat it as a distinct Negro-Roraima (Rio Branco) Arawakan language. The stress statement is based on archival lexical elicitation from what were then among the last speakers; the language is now dormant/extinct.
